question: Why is visiting a patient's home so helpful for disease management?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for any medications.
options.B: It guarantees that the patient will never need a hospital visit.
options.C: It allows nurses to observe real-world habits and living conditions.
options.D: It places the entire workload on family members instead.

explanation: You get a true picture when you see where patients actually live! Home care lets you spot daily habits and environmental factors that directly affect their health. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h1)

question: How does home care primarily change the way healthcare is delivered?

options.A: From hospital-centered interventions to daily life
options.B: From professional nursing to family-only treatment
options.C: From chronic disease management to acute surgery
options.D: From everyday living to rigid facility schedules

explanation: Instead of keeping care locked inside hospital walls, home nursing brings support directly into the patient's personal living space. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h1)

question: Which of these is a great example of primary prevention in the home?

options.A: Performing range-of-motion exercises for a stroke survivor
options.B: Checking blood sugar levels to find early diabetes
options.C: Giving a seasonal flu vaccine to a healthy client
options.D: Treating an open pressure ulcer on the heel

explanation: Primary prevention stops illnesses before they even start. Giving a vaccine to a healthy person is a classic way to protect them! [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h2)

question: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention?

options.A: To reduce complications and manage established chronic illnesses
options.B: To prevent a disease from ever occurring in a healthy person
options.C: To screen a population for hidden risk factors
options.D: To cure acute infections using high-dose antibiotics

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after a disease is already there—helping patients manage symptoms, avoid complications, and live their best daily life. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h2)

question: When checking a home for safety, which of these is a common physical hazard?
explanation: Watch out for loose rugs! They are physical hazards that easily cause elderly patients to trip and fall at home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h3)

question: A nurse notices a dark hallway and no grab bars in the shower. What type of assessment is this?
explanation: Spotting physical risks like poor lighting or missing bathroom grab bars is part of a home environmental safety check. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h3)

question: What daily measurement is most crucial for a home care patient with heart failure?
explanation: Daily weighing is a lifesaver for heart failure patients. It helps catch hidden fluid buildup early before serious breathing problems start. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h4)

question: Why is teaching patients to spot early warning signs of their chronic disease so important?

options.A: It completely cures chronic conditions like diabetes.
options.B: It ensures family members take over all nursing duties.
options.C: It stops patients from ever taking prescription drugs.
options.D: It allows for early action before emergency hospitalization is needed.

explanation: When patients recognize small changes early, they can call for help or adjust care before a scary health crisis lands them in the hospital. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h4)

question: Which handy tool do home care nurses often use to help patients manage multiple daily pills?
explanation: A weekly pill box is a simple lifesaver! It sorts medications by days and times, helping patients stay on track. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h5)

question: Why do many older home care patients struggle to take their medications correctly?

options.A: They have too many extra financial resources.
options.C: Doctors always prescribe only one pill per day.
options.D: Medication bottles are always too easy to open.

explanation: When a patient has too many pills with different rules (some before meals, some at bedtime), it gets super confusing. Keeping it simple is key! [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop infections from spreading in home care?
explanation: Good old-fashioned handwashing is your best defense! It removes germs and stops them from passing between you and your patients. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h6)

question: Which of these is a common myth about infection control in home settings?

options.A: That handwashing helps reduce bacterial spread
options.B: That family members can transmit respiratory viruses
options.C: That the home environment is naturally germ-free
options.D: That used needles require special puncture-proof containers

explanation: Don't be fooled—homes are not naturally sterile! Good cleaning and hygiene habits are still a must everywhere. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the purpose of using the 'teach-back' method during patient education?

options.A: Asking the patient to repeat instructions in their own words
options.B: Testing the patient on medical history terminology
options.C: Reading a medical textbook aloud to the family
options.D: Having the nurse lecture for an hour without stopping

explanation: Teach-back is brilliant: you ask them to explain your instructions back to you in their own words so you know they truly understand. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h7)

question: Why should nurses actively involve family caregivers in disease management education?

options.A: It removes all responsibility from the professional nurse.
options.B: It helps caregivers spot red flags and offer safe daily support.
options.C: It prevents the patient from ever speaking to a doctor.
options.D: It ensures the family takes over financial medical costs.

explanation: Family members are with the patient every day. Training them means someone is always watching for warning signs when you aren't there. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h7)

question: Which healthcare professional do home care nurses often team up with to improve patient mobility?
explanation: Physical therapists are fantastic partners! They work alongside nurses to help patients build strength, balance, and safely move around at home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h8)

question: What is a key part of emergency preparedness in a home care plan?

options.A: Disconnecting all medical equipment to save electricity
options.B: Waiting for the annual checkup to report severe symptoms
options.C: Knowing who to call and what steps to take during a sudden crisis
options.D: Relying solely on neighbors for medical decisions

explanation: When an emergency strikes, panic shouldn't take over. Having a clear plan of who to call keeps both the patient and family safe. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h8)
